author: David Swanson
title: Beyond Borders: Building Community in the Face of Displacement
content:
Africa, Bigotry, Chapters, Endangerment, Events, How I Became a Peace Activist, Immorality, Isingiro Nakivale Chapter, World

By Norbert Byambo Kagosi with Mujib Abid, Peace Voice, October 22, 2026

Forced and involuntary displacement can have many causes. I fled my country for many reasons, including insecurity, persistent conflict, and hatred in my village. In my hometown of Kiliba, in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), life had become unbearable. People could be killed brutally, as if their lives had no value. Nobody knew who would be the next victim or when the violence would strike again.

Completing my diploma in 2018 put a target on my back. Rebels did not want to see someone who had studied and gained an education. What should have been a moment of pride gradually became a source of fear as my life was threatened.

One night, I heard voices outside our house. The people were threatening to kill everyone, saying that nobody would be left alive, not even a child. Those words filled me with terror. They opened the door to my parents’ house and then came directly to the room where I was sleeping. I had no time to think about what to take with me or where I would go. I escaped through a window and ran for my life.

My country has been plagued by violent conflict over the past three decades, fueled by armed groups and foreign interference, rooted in struggles for control of the DRC’s rich mineral resources. A primary example of the so-called ‘resource curse’ phenomenon, the DRC has become a battleground for geopolitical rivalry, caught up in resource grabs by outside powers. Ten million Congolese have perished, and 6.9 million have been displaced, like myself, making the DRC one of the countries most affected by forced displacement in the world.

I traveled from village to village seeking safety. Over the course of two months, I made my way on foot to the Nakivale Refugee Settlement in Uganda, carrying my fear, my pain, and the little hope I still had. I did not choose to become a refugee. I chose to survive. I left behind my home, my community, and the life I had imagined for myself. I wanted a chance to wake up without fear, to continue learning, and to have a future in which my life and my education would not put me in danger.

Since then, I have been working as a peacebuilder, social educator, and conflict resolution trainer in the refugee camps in Uganda, co-founding New Talent for the Best Future in 2020 to empower fellow refugees and uplift vulnerable communities. In today’s global climate of heightened geopolitical conflict, militarization of borders, and increasing violence and hostility towards migrants, it feels radical to say that every human being deserves peace, dignity, education, and the opportunity to live without fear.

Norbert’s experience raises questions that concern us both as peacebuilders. In particular, when the reasons for seeking asylum, in the face of threats of physical harm at home and ever-securitized border regimes, are closely intertwined with the desire for education, self-actualization and seeking change.

Life as a refugee is painful and unfair. But it can also prove transformative. Norbert’s account challenges the tendency to see refugees only through the violence they have endured, overlooking the knowledge, relationships and organizations they build.

The modern border is not simply a line separating one country from another. It is a political instrument, one shaped by empire, racial hierarchy, and a capitalist world system that has never distributed mobility equally. Borders allow weapons and capital to circulate with remarkable freedom, while people displaced by war, coloniality, economic inequality, and climate change are detained, deported or denied safety and protection. The same powers that help produce displacement frequently reserve for themselves the authority to decide who may cross, who must remain, and where each person belongs.

This month, on October 23-25, Norbert will be speaking at the global online conference, #NoWar2026: Beyond Borders, to share his story alongside dozens of other speakers from around the world. I will moderate the panel, ‘Migration is Beautiful,’ bringing together leading writers and activists to make the case for freedom of movement and explore migration as a source of creativity, connection and collective possibility.

We’ll unpack how war and violent conflict uproot communities, how border regimes operate, and most importantly, what a border-free world could look like. What might become possible if people possessed both the freedom to move and the freedom to remain? What if migration were understood not as a threat to be contained, but as an enduring expression of human life?

In Nakivale, Norbert’s work as a peacebuilder, educator and co-founder of New Talent for the Best Future is part of an ongoing effort to build a future with fellow refugees. Displacement has shaped this work, but it does not exhaust the possibilities of his life or theirs. As we look towards Beyond Borders, we ask what becomes possible when displaced people are recognized as organizers, educators and political actors, with a voice in shaping the conditions of our shared world.

Norbert Byambo Kagosi is the Coordinator of the Isingiro Nakivale chapter of World BEYOND War.

Dr Mujib Abid, a member of the Board of World BEYOND War, is an Australia-based scholar-activist and community peacebuilder.

content:

By Omar Mboob, World BEYOND War Gambia Chapter Coordinator, October 18, 2026

World BEYOND War Gambia chapter organized a Multi-stakeholder community dialogue on disarmament and peace on 17 October 2026, at the National Youth Council Hall in Banjul, The Gambia. The event brought together 20 participants, including youth leaders, students, women representatives, grassroots organizers, and civil society representatives, to discuss the proliferation of small arms and light weapons, community security, nonviolent conflict prevention, and youth participation in peacebuilding. The dialogue took place against the backdrop of security concerns associated with illicit arms trafficking, particularly around the Foni region and the cross-border corridor linking The Gambia and Senegal’s Casamance region. Participants emphasized the importance of peaceful coexistence, community engagement, and constructive dialogue in preventing violence and promoting national development.

A central theme of the dialogue was the need to address the proliferation of weapons while strengthening communities’ capacity to prevent violence. Participants discussed how young people can challenge attitudes that normalize violence, promote nonviolent alternatives, and take an active role in their communities in order to contribute to peacebuilding. title: The One Big Peace Conference and Open Borders
content:
Nonviolent Activism, What to do, Why End War, World

By David Swanson, World BEYOND War, October 16, 2026

Approximately once a day for forever, so approximately 365 times a year, someone proposes to me the same good idea. Hey, they suggest, I’d like to organize one big peace conference and create one big peace movement to unite everyone and be stronger instead of fractured.

I have several answers. First and foremost is: hell yeah, great idea, do it! do it! do it!

Another answer is: there are reasons the 364 other people who’ve said this to me this year have not actually done it, just like the 365 who thought of it last year. It costs lots of money. It’s harder to get people to a conference than to a rally or a protest. There are language barriers. Whoever is in charge of organizing it will be assumed by others to not be totally welcoming of their views. There will be at least some truth to that, since no two people completely agree on everything. If you have this one big conference for everyone in a physical location, as 90 percent of you with this idea want, it will be closer and easier to get to for some people than for others. Maybe we should attempt a regional one for some people. Etc. Etc.

But once a year, I like to focus on a different answer, this one: I don’t have time to do yours for you because I’m already doing it.

It is not possible to excuse, justify, or condone this kind of rhetoric. The only question is what to do about it.

Of all of the things that Donald Trump has said publicly since returning to the White House, his threats to annihilate Iran are arguably the worst. This is not only because the repeated statements are deeply immoral and illegal–deliberate killing of civilians is a war crime–but because they represent the kind of irresponsible rhetoric that will lead us into a global apocalypse and collapse of not just the Persian nation but human civilization as a whole. It is not possible to excuse, justify, or condone this kind of rhetoric. The only question is what to do about it.

By Karl Grossman, CounterPunch, October 9, 2026

The lead front page story in the New York Times this week was headlined: “Superpowers Racing to Put Nuclear Reactors on Moon.” The nations involved: the U.S., China and Russia. And there was a subhead: “Experts Warn of Radioactive Risks From a Rocket Mishap or Lunar Meltdown.”

The reporter, Selam Gebrekidan, wrote: “Failures could cause a chain reaction with dire consequences. Falling reactor debris could scatter radioactive material….An explosion or a meltdown on the moon’s surface could risk turning entire regions into no-go zones.”

The extensive story quoted Edward Lyman, director of nuclear power safety at the Union of Concerned Scientists, saying: “There will always be a space race going on, and if you enter nuclear power into that mix, then it could take a potentially more dangerous turn.”

Nuclear power and weapons in space have been an unexpectedly extensive part of my journalistic journey. Because of having been deeply involved in reporting about the plans of the Long Island Lighting Company to construct seven to 11 nuclear power plants on Long Island, where I live, I became knowledgeable about atomic energy.

title: Books or Bombs? France’s Student Revolt vs. NATO’s Spending Push
content:
By 

Medea Benjamin

, October 8, 2026




For the third week in a row, high school students across France are taking to the streets demanding more investment in their education. They want more teachers, smaller classes, decent school buildings and a public education system that works for poor and working-class students.




But their struggle comes at a moment when France faces mounting pressure to cut public spending while dramatically increasing its military budget. The question at the heart of this uprising goes far beyond education: Will France invest in its young people—or in missiles, weapons and war? Books or bombs?




What began in the Paris suburbs has spread to more than a thousand schools. On October 6, more than 250,000 people reportedly took to the streets in demonstrations supporting the students.




The government’s response has only deepened the anger. Instead of addressing students’ demands, authorities have unleashed riot police, tear gas, grenades and mass arrests. More than 6,500 people have reportedly been arrested since the protests began, most of them minors. Some young protesters have suffered horrific injuries, including a 15-year-old who lost his hand after a police grenade exploded. Amnesty International has condemned what it calls the “disproportionate” use of force against young people peacefully demanding their right to education.

By David Swanson, World BEYOND War, October 3, 2026




Remarks in Baltimore on October 3, 2026, at event with 

War Is Still A Lie




Thank you to Ronda Cooperstein and the local chapter of World BEYOND War for setting this event up.




I recently read a big stack of books on the decline and elimination of dueling. There were thousands of factors, many of them beyond anyone’s easy control, but key among them was cultural change, was bringing people to find greater humiliation in dueling than in not dueling, greater respect in refusing to duel than in being willing to duel. The picture of dueling as noble, respectable, and courageous was replaced by one much nearer the truth: drunken primadonnas misperceiving insults and committing murder for lack of the ability to admit they were idiots. And dueling died by stages. More and more would-be duelists’ so-called seconds negotiated peace. More and more duels ended without deaths or injuries, often with bullets intentionally shot into the air. More and more duelists were prosecuted for the crime. More and more newspaper cartoonists depicted duelists as monkeys and clowns. Dueling was outlawed and denounced for centuries before the abolitionists finally succeeded.

Education shapes how we understand peace, conflict, security and war; what futures we can imagine; and what we believe we can change.

There was already widespread opposition to Trump’s proposed arch at Memorial Circle in Arlington, Virginia—a 250-foot structure, roughly the height of a 20-story building and 50 percent taller than Paris’s Arc de Triomphe. Now the controversy has intensified: Trump says the arch, which originally included plans for an observation deck, a café, a gift shop and exhibition space, would also function as a military complex, housing drones, snipers and ammunition.

Here are 10 reasons (really 9 plus your own) to oppose the “Arc de Trump.”

1. It would overwhelm one of America’s most important historic landscapes. The giant arch would sit directly on the ceremonial axis connecting Arlington House, Arlington National Cemetery, Memorial Bridge and the Lincoln Memorial, dramatically altering this historic view and dwarfing the surrounding monuments rather than complementing them.

2. It clashes with the very meaning of the site. Arlington Memorial Bridge and the surrounding landscape were conceived as symbols of national reconciliation after the Civil War. Wednesday morning I was speaking by Zoom to a college class about war and peace, and one of the students asked about the risk of the U.S. demilitarizing and other nations not. I gave a standard answer about how a reverse arms race could be done in stages. The U.S. could commit to not spending more than three times any other nation on its military and proceed downward from there. Of the couple of dozen nations that spend much of anything on their militaries, all but three are U.S. allies and weapons customers being hammered hard by the U.S. government (and NATO) to spend more. The only country spending more than a tiny fraction of the U.S. — in fact, spending close to a third of U.S. military spending as it’s usually reported or a sixth of what it really is — is China. If the U.S. were to keep its nukes out of South Korea and Japan, and its troops out of South Korea, and finally end the war and turn South Korea’s military over to South Korea, and start joining treaties and courts and beginning a general disarmament, North Korea would almost certainly join in serious negotiations about getting rid of its nukes, while China would — I guaranteed to this college class — not keep increasing its own military spending.

author: David Swanson
title: One Down! Abolishing Dueling and Warmaking
content:
By David Swanson, World BEYOND War, September 29, 2026




According to an 1838 U.S.-published instruction manual for dueling, the practice of dueling was going to last “as long as a manly independence, and a lofty personal pride in all that dignifies and ennobles the human character, shall continue to exist.”[1] Be that as it may, dueling was soon gone as a practice in any way acceptable or routine, and most of the globe had never had it to begin with.




Many years ago, I wrote a book about the outlawrists of the 1920s, people (led by lawyers) who were fond of pointing out that dueling had been outlawed and abolished, and so could war be. Yet dueling had persisted for centuries in Europe and in the United States despite laws forbidding it as murder. And we’ve now gone a century with laws forbidding war, while the wars persist.




I do not doubt for a minute that laws helped end dueling. Nobody could have finally begun using the laws had there not been any. Nobody could have denounced dueling as a crime had it not been a crime. But I’ve encountered over the years numerous cursory accounts of dueling that explain its demise in very simple terms, albeit each explanation different from all the others.
